title.en: Support solvability claims with a solution or proof

summary: Use a valid solution to establish solvability and a complete proof, certificate or sound search for impossibility or uniqueness; report bounded search as unknown.
objective: Match a solvability or hint claim to a method capable of establishing it.
applies_when: A packing, tiling or placement puzzle offers hints, a solution or a solvability statement.
The scene reports that no solution exists.
A generator produces puzzles that are asserted to be solvable.
example_prompts: Generate a packing puzzle that is guaranteed solvable and can hint.
Tell me whether this arrangement can still be completed.
negative_signals: Open-ended building where no completion condition exists.
Claims unsupported by a valid solution, complete proof or sound search; a search budget alone cannot establish impossibility.
not_for: Open-ended building where no completion condition exists.
Claims unsupported by a valid solution, complete proof or sound search; a search budget alone cannot establish impossibility.

principles: Solvable and unsolvable are different claims with different costs. One completed solution proves solvability. Impossibility needs a proof: a complete search whose pruning provably preserves all solutions, a certificate from a solver, or an argument such as a colouring, parity or area invariant that rules out every arrangement without enumerating them.

Packing and tiling puzzles are naturally expressed as exact cover, where each cell must be covered exactly once and each piece used according to its rule, and depth-first backtracking with efficient undo of local structure is the classical method for enumerating solutions to such problems.

Generating a puzzle from a known solution is the cheap way to guarantee solvability, but it says nothing about uniqueness, which needs either a complete search or an argument that no second solution exists.
Hints must come from the search over the current state, not from the generator solution, otherwise a hint can contradict legal moves the player has already made.
implementation: Model the puzzle as a covering problem over cells and pieces, so the same search serves solving, hinting and counting.

Generate from a valid solution when useful. Establish uniqueness with either a complete sound search or an independent proof/certificate; any difficulty claim needs its own declared basis rather than following automatically from solvability.
Derive hints from a search rooted at the current state so they remain valid after unusual play.
Bound the search explicitly and report when the bound was reached, since an aborted search is not a proof of unsolvability.
Report what the search covered: all solutions, first solution, or a bounded exploration.
Where an invariant settles the question, state it: a parity, colouring or area argument is a complete proof of impossibility and is usually cheaper and more explanatory than any search.
observable_checks: Place pieces into a dead end and confirm the scene reports either a proven no-completion result or an honest unknown when its search budget expired; a bounded run is not required to reach a conclusive answer, only to say which it reached.
Compare the reported solution count on a small instance with a hand enumeration.
Ask for a hint after an unusual but legal sequence and confirm the hint is consistent with the current state.
Trigger the search bound and confirm the message distinguishes not found from does not exist.

creative_affordances: Showing the search itself, including backtracking, is often a compelling scene in its own right.
Difficulty can be shaped by the generator without weakening the solvability guarantee.
known_limits: Authored guidance citing the exact-cover framing and its classical backtracking technique; it prescribes no implementation and makes no performance claim.
When exhaustive search is impractical, a separate invariant or proof may still settle the claim. Without such evidence, report the unresolved result rather than asserting impossibility or uniqueness.

claims.statement: Puzzle problems such as tiling a tray with a fixed set of polyominoes can be expressed as exact cover problems and solved by depth-first backtracking search that uses reversible local operations on linked structures to undo choices efficiently.
claims.scope: Combinatorial search technique for exact cover formulations; it does not bound the running time for a specific puzzle instance.
